frictionVectors.title: European Energy Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong leverage as a major gas supplier to Europe, but European diversification and renewable investment gradually constrain its negotiating power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment Controls
frictionVectors.details: Strict state participation rules protect national control over hydrocarbons and strategic infrastructure, while limiting technology and capital inflows.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is drawing substantial US and European interest as a route for critical minerals, increasing Angola's strategic value but also external competition over infrastructure governance.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lending remains influential despite restructuring and diversification efforts, while declining oil output limits Luanda's room to build fully autonomous fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border and Transit Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain vulnerable to border insecurity and political disputes, threatening Benin's role as a transit outlet for landlocked Sahelian trade.

frictionVectors.title: External Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's modernization depends on foreign capital and operators, creating efficiency gains while exposing strategic trade infrastructure to outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Relationship
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and domestic beneficiation in its diamond partnership, but remains exposed to weak global diamond demand and foreign marketing networks.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Race
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, rare earths, and other minerals could broaden sovereign resource control, although new projects may bring dependence on external investors and processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking a larger state role and greater domestic processing in gold mining, challenging established foreign operators and raising investor uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russia reduces reliance on France and Western partners but creates new concerns over opaque contracting, accountability, and resource-linked influence.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mineral Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral exports remain vulnerable to informal networks and opaque foreign-linked trading arrangements. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture revenue and enforce traceability.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Political and security tensions with Rwanda constrain trade and increase dependence on alternative regional corridors. Cross-border instability also complicates control of Lake Tanganyika and eastern mineral routes.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cape Verde's ports and air links attract competing European, North American, and Chinese interest because of the archipelago's Atlantic position. The government retains comparatively strong leverage but remains dependent on external capital and tourism.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Desalination, fuel imports, and grid investment leave the country exposed to external price shocks. Renewable expansion improves resilience but has not removed infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state retains formal ownership of hydrocarbons and minerals, but financing, technology, and marketing remain heavily dependent on foreign firms. Contract opacity and weak oversight limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Export Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest regions disrupts local economies and raises security costs around transport and agricultural infrastructure. The Douala-Kribi corridor also faces strategic competition from external infrastructure and logistics actors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security networks retain major influence over regime protection and access to gold and diamond zones. This arrangement strengthens short-term state security while weakening transparency and bargaining power over natural resources.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Resource Areas
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and local intermediaries continue to control or tax parts of the mining economy outside effective state administration. Poor roads and limited public infrastructure make formalization and revenue collection difficult.

highlights: Oil State Balances Sovereignty and Dependence

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the central source of fiscal leverage, but production, financing, and export infrastructure are tied to foreign operators and regional pipelines. This limits diversification and exposes sovereignty to external commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chad's strategic position and counterterrorism role sustain strong outside interest in its military partnerships and airfield infrastructure. Shifting relations with France, Russia-linked actors, and neighboring governments complicate independent security policy.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and Maritime Jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: France's control of Mayotte continues to drive diplomatic friction and limits Comoros' effective control over surrounding maritime resources and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government relies heavily on foreign financing and contractors for ports, energy, and transport, reducing policy autonomy despite efforts to diversify partners.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining firms and trading networks retain major influence over cobalt and copper value chains, while Kinshasa seeks greater local processing and contract leverage.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east, involving armed groups and regional power competition, threatens mining zones, transport routes, and state control of border resources.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export capacity remain heavily dependent on offshore oil, leaving Brazzaville exposed to foreign operators, price cycles, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects provide essential connectivity but reinforce external creditor and contractor influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Commodity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding processing and mining capacity, but international traders and price-setting systems still capture substantial value from cocoa exports.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Influence in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors compete across ports, energy, transport, and mining, creating diversification opportunities alongside dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Base Politics and Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Hosting major foreign military facilities generates revenue and security guarantees but limits Djibouti's room for maneuver amid US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other strategic competition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: China-linked financing and competition over port and logistics assets leave Djibouti vulnerable to debt pressure and external influence over critical trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset concessions
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and Gulf investment provide essential liquidity but increase outside leverage over state assets, infrastructure, and strategic land. Debt-service pressures constrain Cairo's room to protect full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam and water security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over GERD operations remains Egypt's most consequential resource-security risk. Cairo continues diplomatic and security pressure while seeking guarantees against reduced downstream water flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output is weakening state revenue and increasing dependence on foreign technical partners and investment. New gas and offshore projects offer potential but leave Equatorial Guinea exposed to external capital and market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing remain important to transport and public infrastructure. Repayment obligations and opaque contracting can limit domestic oversight of nationally strategic assets.

highlights: Red Sea geography raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb draw sustained interest from Gulf, regional, and global security actors. Foreign military access and maritime competition could generate leverage without delivering broad domestic economic gains.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production relies heavily on foreign partners, technology, and financing. Limited transparency and the dominance of state-linked structures make revenue capture and long-term sovereign control difficult to assess.

highlights: Economic sovereignty tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African trade routes, banking, electricity links, and customs revenues. This provides resilience but limits independent control over logistics, energy security, and regional economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Taiwan-China diplomatic pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's recognition of Taiwan brings development and diplomatic benefits but exposes it to pressure from Beijing and potential shifts in external financing. The relationship also narrows maneuvering space with major infrastructure and trade partners.

highlights: Debt and regional tensions constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: GERD and downstream water politics
frictionVectors.details: The dam improves Ethiopia's potential control over electricity generation and regional energy exports, but unresolved operating arrangements with Egypt and Sudan sustain diplomatic and security risk. Seasonal filling and drought conditions remain especially sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and strategic finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service stress and restructuring negotiations increase Ethiopia's dependence on international lenders and external partners. Gulf, Chinese, Turkish, and Western financing can accelerate infrastructure recovery while competing for influence over ports, energy, and telecommunications.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining leverage
frictionVectors.details: The transition government is seeking greater state participation and local value addition in manganese, iron ore, and oil. Existing French, Chinese, and other commercial interests remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure financing gap
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, and power upgrades are essential for resource sovereignty, but Gabon remains reliant on external capital and technical partners.

highlights: Senegal remains the indispensable security partner
Cashew, fisheries, and port access drive leverage

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's transport, energy, and food-security links with Senegal provide stability but constrain independent economic policy and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime control
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing and limited maritime enforcement weaken control over coastal resources, with foreign fleets benefiting from monitoring gaps.

highlights: Gold and critical-mineral governance under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains the dominant export while illegal mining damages land and water resources. Emerging lithium and bauxite projects intensify debate over royalties, local processing, and foreign investor access.

frictionVectors.title: External financial conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed stabilization and creditor negotiations improve macroeconomic discipline but constrain spending choices and the government's ability to direct resource revenues independently.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over strategic minerals

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor depends heavily on Chinese-led investment, foreign engineering, and export infrastructure. Guinea can capture substantial rents, but operational and financing dependence limits full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Political transition risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government's prolonged transition creates uncertainty over contracts, elections, and investor protections. Resource nationalism may strengthen state bargaining power while increasing diplomatic and commercial friction.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the economic lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's cashew economy, while limited domestic processing leaves producers exposed to external price and logistics decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and political vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political instability make the port, customs system, and offshore resource prospects vulnerable to outside influence and opaque commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-linked fiscal discipline with repayment and commercial pressures tied to major foreign-financed transport projects. Nairobi is seeking greater local control while remaining dependent on external capital for infrastructure expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains central to East African trade, but competition from Tanzanian and Djiboutian corridors is increasing. Foreign investment and security partnerships around logistics infrastructure create recurring sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Water sovereignty tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide essential revenue but deepen dependence on South Africa, which finances and receives the bulk of the resource. Delays, compensation disputes, and unequal bargaining power remain persistent concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Economic Dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, employment, customs revenue, and security ties leave Maseru with limited room to diversify its external partnerships. Mining and textile sectors remain vulnerable to external market and policy shifts.

highlights: Infrastructure recovery depends on foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-operated iron ore projects generate exports and employment but concentrate bargaining power outside the state. Revenue transparency, local-content obligations, and infrastructure commitments remain central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia relies on foreign operators and donors to rehabilitate ports, roads, and energy systems. This improves connectivity but can lock strategic infrastructure into concession arrangements with limited domestic financing alternatives.

highlights: Foreign security patrons shape state authority

frictionVectors.title: Oil Governance Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Competing political authorities and armed groups can disrupt production, exports, and budget flows through the National Oil Corporation. Control over terminals and revenue allocation remains a core source of internal and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, and other external actors maintain influence through security partnerships, contractors, and political networks. Their involvement limits unified Libyan control over strategic territory, bases, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining operations anchor export earnings but expose Madagascar to external pricing, financing, and operational decisions. Fiscal returns and environmental costs remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Infrastructure Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign companies and lenders play a major role in power, transport, and extractive infrastructure. Weak state capacity and contested land rights can reduce Madagascar's ability to enforce local-content and environmental protections.

highlights: Critical minerals drive new foreign interest

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: Prospective graphite, rare-earth and uranium projects could bring foreign capital but risk weak bargaining power and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel constrain industrial sovereignty, while external lenders shape infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over gold sector
Russian security ties replace Western partnerships

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state share of gold revenues, but insecurity, opaque contracting and foreign operators complicate effective control.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The shift toward Russian security support has reduced Western influence while increasing dependence on an external military partner amid worsening instability.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers new fiscal and diplomatic leverage, but revenue-sharing and operator dependence limit near-term autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: MINING LOGISTICS
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports remain tied to foreign capital, rail infrastructure and global prices, leaving the state vulnerable to supply-chain and financing pressures.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty dispute and future arrangements for Diego Garcia remain central to Mauritius's strategic autonomy and relations with the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL ENERGY EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported fuel leaves the island vulnerable to shipping disruptions, although renewable investment is gradually improving resilience.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables strengthen strategic leverage
Atlantic infrastructure links Africa and Europe

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCES
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and prospective offshore resources remain tied to the Western Sahara dispute, generating legal and diplomatic pressure from external actors.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN INFRASTRUCTURE CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf and Chinese investment supports ports, rail and renewables but creates exposure to competing external strategic interests.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security remains the LNG gatekeeper
Gas sovereignty constrained by foreign capital and stalled megaprojects

frictionVectors.title: LNG project vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and persistent insecurity in Cabo Delgado continue to delay or raise the cost of major liquefied natural gas projects. International operators retain substantial control over financing, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique relies on regional and international security assistance to protect energy corridors and offshore investments, limiting fully autonomous control over strategic assets.

highlights: Green hydrogen ambitions meet infrastructure constraints

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: International firms are competing for uranium, lithium, rare earths, and other minerals, creating opportunities for investment but also pressure to export raw materials before domestic processing capacity is established.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen and port dependency
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen projects depend heavily on foreign capital, imported technology, and upgraded power and port infrastructure. Walvis Bay and associated transport corridors are becoming strategically important to outside partners.

highlights: Uranium and oil exports are being reoriented

frictionVectors.title: French exit and Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced French influence and deepened security ties with Russia, while still struggling to translate political sovereignty into effective territorial security and economic resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Border closures and energy disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with ECOWAS neighbors and border restrictions have disrupted trade, fuel access, and external supply routes. Dependence on limited export corridors leaves Niger vulnerable to political pressure from neighboring states.

highlights: Oil sovereignty is undermined by theft and underinvestment
Gas and refining capacity are being rebuilt domestically

frictionVectors.title: Oil theft and foreign-operator leverage
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline theft, sabotage, and insecurity in the Niger Delta continue to reduce public revenue and weaken state control over production. International oil companies retain significant influence over technology, financing, and legacy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and gas infrastructure bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could reduce fuel-import dependence, but unreliable power, transport constraints, and regulatory uncertainty continue to limit the strategic benefits of Nigeria's large hydrocarbon base.

highlights: State capacity remains high but regionally contested
Mineral-export credibility faces scrutiny over eastern Congo links

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo mineral and security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate sustained diplomatic pressure and threaten its reputation as a rules-based investment hub.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and investment dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda exercises strong domestic control over strategic planning, but remains reliant on foreign aid, concessional finance, and external investment for infrastructure and growth. Shifts in Western policy could narrow its room for maneuver.

highlights: Offshore hydrocarbons remain prospective, not yet transformative
Maritime security and external financing shape strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Offshore Claims
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is balancing oil exploration interests with maritime-boundary sensitivities and limited technical capacity. External energy firms and neighboring coastal states retain significant leverage over any future development.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on Portuguese, European, Chinese, and multilateral support for infrastructure and public finance. This limits bargaining power over transport and energy projects.

highlights: Oil and gas production strengthens fiscal leverage
Debt pressure tests control over new resource revenues

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Governance and Debt
frictionVectors.details: Sangomar oil and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project offer greater sovereign leverage, but high debt and financing needs may constrain how revenues are managed. Contract transparency and local-content expectations remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Casamance and Regional Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Casamance conflict is substantially quieter but still affects perceptions of territorial integration and investment risk. Energy, port, and transport projects also remain exposed to external lenders and operators.

highlights: Strategic competition surrounds ports and ocean surveillance

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles is seeking balanced ties with India, China, the United States, and European partners while avoiding militarization of its territory. Port access, coast-guard cooperation, and surveillance infrastructure are sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Maritime Resource Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access remains economically important but creates enforcement and sustainability risks. Limited patrol capacity leaves the exclusive economic zone dependent on external monitoring and security partnerships.

highlights: Mining drives growth but limits domestic value capture
Ports and logistics attract competing foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects provide revenue and employment but expose Sierra Leone to commodity cycles and foreign operators. Local processing and fiscal enforcement remain weaker than the country’s resource potential.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: External firms and financiers are central to port, road, and mining-corridor development. The government must balance Chinese and Western-linked investment while protecting public revenue and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Federal sovereignty remains contested across the territory
Red Sea and offshore resources intensify external competition

frictionVectors.title: Horn of Africa Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Somalia’s disputes with Somaliland and Ethiopia over maritime access continue to constrain control of territory and coastal assets. Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and other partners hold significant influence over security, ports, and political networks.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Energy and Security Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas resources attract foreign contractors before Somalia has fully consolidated regulatory and security capacity. Fragmented authority, Al-Shabaab insurgency, and competing port arrangements create major risks to sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port congestion continue to constrain domestic control over mining exports. Reform of Eskom and Transnet is improving the outlook but remains vulnerable to fiscal and political delays.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL INFLUENCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: China, the United States, and European states are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals. Pretoria is balancing investment needs against pressure to preserve beneficiation and nonalignment.

highlights: Oil revenues remain hostage to regional war

frictionVectors.title: VULNERABLE OIL PIPELINE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production and state revenues exposed to sabotage, transit disputes, and foreign operator leverage.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE AND FOREIGN RESOURCE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and contested security arrangements limit public control over oil proceeds. Chinese and other external firms remain important to production while political factions compete over revenue allocation.

highlights: Gold and ports anchor external competition

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Competing military authorities and cross-border trading networks continue to divert gold revenues away from civilian institutions. External buyers and alleged foreign logistical support deepen the country’s extractive dependency.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and associated maritime infrastructure has strategic value for regional and international powers. The conflict risks turning port access, aid routes, and future mineral corridors into bargaining assets.

highlights: LNG and mining policy regain momentum

frictionVectors.title: LNG NEGOTIATION BALANCE
frictionVectors.details: Prospective gas development could strengthen state revenues and industrial capacity, but contract terms, local content, and environmental safeguards remain central sovereignty concerns as international energy firms re-enter.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign financing is reshaping ports and railway corridors serving Tanzania and its landlocked neighbors. These projects improve connectivity while creating long-term exposure to external creditors and operators.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics pivot

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCY
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major trade and transshipment hub, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign capital, shipping networks, and external commercial partners. This limits policy room over strategic logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity along the northern frontier are increasing pressure for foreign training, intelligence, and security assistance. Expanded dependence on outside partners could complicate sovereign control of border policy.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION AND FINANCE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: European financial and migration partnerships provide essential support but increase Tunisian dependence on external policy priorities. IMF-linked fiscal reforms remain politically difficult and constrain domestic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY IMPORT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported hydrocarbons exposes Tunisia to price shocks and external supply leverage. Phosphate-sector weakness further limits export earnings and state control over strategic revenue.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP AND OIL SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The EACOP project promises export revenue and infrastructure but places Uganda's petroleum future within a foreign-led consortium and transit route through Tanzania. Financing, environmental opposition, and sanctions-related scrutiny continue to raise sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-BACKED INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, energy, and industrial projects expands state capacity while increasing exposure to repayment and procurement obligations. Kampala is balancing Chinese capital against Western governance pressure and regional security commitments.

frictionVectors.title: COPPER OWNERSHIP AND VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: New investment from Western, Gulf, and Chinese-linked firms is accelerating copper production, but Zambia still faces limited domestic processing and bargaining power. Fiscal stability depends on converting mineral expansion into reliable public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: POWER SUPPLY BOTTLENECK
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages constrain mining output and expose the economy to climate variability. Emergency imports and new generation partnerships could improve resilience but may deepen dependence on external capital and regional grids.

frictionVectors.title: LITHIUM AND MINERAL LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and local-processing requirements to capture more value from lithium and other minerals, but foreign firms retain major advantages in finance, technology, and market access. Chinese-linked investment remains particularly influential.

frictionVectors.title: CURRENCY AND SANCTIONS CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Persistent currency instability and restricted access to international finance weaken the government's ability to fund infrastructure and enforce resource terms. Sanctions and creditor disputes continue to push Harare toward selective reliance on non-Western partners.
